Project 01 / 04
AIDA Tech / Audio Landing Page

Focus Headphones

Selling premium noise-cancelling headphones to a generation that's never been more distracted — by making the product story about reclaiming attention, not audio specs.

Audience
Young adults, 18–30
Goal
Drive purchases
Format
Landing page copy
Specialty
Direct response

The angle

Open with the enemy, not the product: notifications, horns, minor distractions — the small thefts of focus everyone recognizes instantly. The headphones only enter the story as the way out.

The mechanism

A repeated triplet — "Every notification. Every horn. Every minor…" — builds rhythm and irritation before the release line drops the tension. Feature tiles stay benefit-first: comfort and immersion, not specs.

Why it works

The headline does Attention and Interest work simultaneously by dramatizing a feeling the reader is already having mid-scroll. By the time "deserve your full immersion" appears, Desire is already built — the close just has to confirm the offer.

Project 02 / 04
AIDA Premium Goods Landing Page

The Last Work Bag

Positioning a handcrafted leather bag as a one-time investment rather than another purchase in a cycle of replacements — for a buyer who's been burned before.

Audience
Career-driven professionals
Goal
Justify a premium price
Format
Landing page copy
Specialty
Direct response

The angle

"Buy your last work bag first" reframes the purchase as an exit from a cycle, not an entry into one. It's a promise of finality — rare and valuable in a category built on planned obsolescence.

The mechanism

First-impression psychology opens the piece — "they've already formed an impression" — before the bag is even mentioned. Four short icon-led beats carry the reader from problem to craftsmanship to commitment.

Why it works

Premium goods sell on the cost of not buying them. By detailing exactly how cheaper bags fail — corners wearing, shape collapsing — the copy makes the higher price feel like the cautious choice, not the indulgent one.

Project 03 / 04
AIDA Education Landing Page

Speak English With Confidence

Converting the quiet embarrassment of "freezing up" in English into course sign-ups — against a competitor set the audience already associates with years of slow, boring progress.

Audience
Young adults, 18–30
Goal
Course sign-ups
Format
Landing page copy
Specialty
Direct response

The angle

Name the real cost — not "imperfect English," but the job, the opportunity, the conversation that didn't happen because of it. The ask is never "learn English"; it's "stop putting your life on hold."

The mechanism

A three-step "good news" structure removes the two biggest objections — time and boredom — before asking for the sign-up, and "1,000+ learners" supplies social proof right at the close.

Why it works

This is the page where urgency and warmth have to coexist — the visual leads with stress, the copy answers with reassurance. Keeping that balance consistent is what keeps the page from feeling like two pitches stitched together.

Project 04 / 04
AIDA Fintech / App Landing Page

The $47 Problem

Driving downloads for a personal-finance app aimed at a generation that doesn't lack income so much as visibility into where it goes.

Audience
Young adults, 18–30
Goal
App downloads
Format
Landing page copy
Specialty
Direct response

The angle

Open on a real, specific number — "$47, and the month isn't over" — instead of a vague promise about saving money. Specificity is what makes the scenario feel like a screenshot of the reader's own bank app.

The mechanism

The copy explicitly removes blame — "it's not your income, it's not bad luck" — before naming the real cause, so the reader can accept the diagnosis without feeling judged. That's what clears the path to "download."

Why it works

"You're flying blind" reframes the whole category: this isn't a discipline problem, it's an information problem — turning a budgeting app from a chore into a dashboard the reader actually wants installed.
